#### Rebar Detailing Options for Column Stacks  [Menus/Detailing/Rebar_Detailing_Options_for_Column_Stacks.htm]
Rebar Detailing Options for Column Stacks Rebar Detailing Options for Columns Click the Detailing menu > Bar Selection and Curtailment Rule > Column Stack Bar Selection and Curtailment Rule command to display the Bar Selection and Curtailment rule form for column stacks. Use this form to set how reinforced concrete columns should be detailed and displayed in the detailing drawings. Important Note: It is recommended that these rules be set before detailing the model. If the detailing has already been run and changes to these rules are made, when detailing is re-run the program will prompt the user to (a) run the detailing and generate a new set of drawings or (b) synchronize the detailing and update only the items on the existing drawings that are affected by the detailing changes. Note: Bar Selection and Curtailment Rules can also be changed from within the Detailing Editor. Vertical Bar Layout These options related to the main vertical bars of the column layout. Use Layout Specified in Section Definition: When this option is selected, the program will start by using the basic reinforcement layout defined in the definition of the concrete frame section . Keep Sizes (and numbers same as section definition) vs Select Sizes (to satisfy required As/Ratio): Choosing between these option to specify whether the program keeps the exact bar size and layout in the section definition or whether ETABS is free to optimize bar sizes while maintaining the basic layout from the section definition. Automatically Select Bar Layout (using Bar Selection Rules): Use this option to have ETABS automatically select the bar layout. Prefer Larger Bar Number vs Prefer Larger Bar Size: Choosing between these options will bias the bar optimization routine in ETABS in how it increases the total bar area in the column. Transverse Tie Layout Use the options on this area to specify how the transverse shear reinforcing should be detailed for the columns. Use Layout Specified in Section Definition: When this option is selected, the program will start by using the basic reinforcement layout defined in the definition of the concrete frame section . Automatically Select to Match Vertical Bars and Rules: These options will change the size of the transverse ties based on code requirements related to the selected vertical bars. Enforce User Reinforcement Use these options to enter user specified minimum maximum reinforcement ratios for the column. Rebar Selection Rules This button will open the Rebar Selection Rules form which allows you to control the types of bars that are selected for your column. Bar types and zones refer to the bars in the column elevation for specific location and curtailment. These do not refer to the bar layers. Bar Sizes: The Smallest Bar Size, Largest Bar Sizes , and the Preferred Bar Size can be specified for the different vertical bars or the different in the column. to view the Bar Type Definitions. Note: To add more bar sizes to the drop-down lists, go to Define menu > Section Properties > Reinforcing Bar Sizes. Bar Numbers and Spacing: Minimum and Maximum Number of Bars for each Bar Type can be specified by selecting from the drop-down list. The spacing factors for the ties can be specified by directly entering the values into the text boxes. Notes: When area of the specified Preferred Bar Size is insufficient during detailing and in such cases if selection of a higher bar size is desired rather than increasing Bar Number , the user must specify Maximum Number of Bars for the required Bar Type. Bar Splicing This button will open the Bar Splices form which allows you to specify information that is used for splicing the column vertical bars. This includes the following: Splice Location in Story - The bars may be spliced right at the floor level or at mid height. Splice Type - This drop down allows you to specify what type of splice is used for the column stack. . Splice and Embed Length Factors - This drop down list allows you to determine the splice and embed lengths. Minimum Splice Length - This should self explanatory as it allows you to enter in a user defined minimum splice length.

#### Rebar Detailing Options for Slabs/Mats/Footings  [Menus/Detailing/Rebar_Detailing_Options_for_Slabs_Mats_Footings.htm]
Rebar Detailing Options for Slabs/Mats/Footings Rebar Detailing Options for Slabs / Mats / Footings Click the Detailing menu > Bar Selection and Curtailment Rule > Slab / Mat / Footing Bar Selection and Curtailment Rule command to display the Bar Selection and Curtailment rule form for slabs, mats, and footings. Use this form to set how reinforced concrete slabs, mats or footings should be detailed and displayed in the detailing drawings. Note: It is recommended that these rules be set before detailing the model. If the detailing has already been run and changes to these rules are made, when detailing is re-run the program will prompt the user to (a) run the detailing and generate a new set of drawings or (b) synchronize the detailing and update only the items on the existing drawings that are affected by the detailing changes. Rebar Curtailment Options Use Computed Reinforcement Only: When this option is selected, the program determines the bar location and length based solely on the reinforcement computed from analysis and design. Curtail Alternate Bars: Check this box to curtail the reinforcement at the location where 50% of the bars are no longer required from the analysis and design results. Add Development Length: Check this box to add on development length to the bar locations calculated. Note: Using the Use Computed Reinforcement Only option may produce reinforcement layout quite different from the Use Computed Reinforcement and Curtailment Rules option in which curtailment rules are used together with computed reinforcement. This option should be used with caution and when manual checking and editing of reinforcement is expected. Use Curtailment Rules Only: This option is NOT available for Mats or Footings. It forces the detailing routine to ignore the computed reinforcement and base the bar selection on the curtailment rules only. Note: Using the Use Curtailment Rules Only option may produce reinforcement layout quite different from the Use Computed Reinforcement and Curtailment Rules option in which curtailment rules are used together with computed reinforcement. This option should be used with caution and when manual checking and editing of reinforcement is expected. Use Computed Reinforcement and Curtailment Rules: This option is NOT available for Mats or Footings. When this option is selected, the program computes the size and number of required bars at critical locations (top of support and mid span and so forth). It then checks the minimum and maximum number of bars and the like. A theoretical cut off location is determined for each bar. The curtailment location is then computed based on the specified rules and the governing bar location and length are selected. Check Development Length: When this box is checked the required development length/overlap length is calculated and added to the cut off location determined for each bar. Development Length Button: This button will open the Bar Development Rules form which allows you to specify information that affects a given bar's development length (coating, concrete type, etc) Curtailment Rules Button: This button will open the Slab Rebar Curtailment Rules form . This option is NOT available for Mats or Footings. Note: The rebar location and length determined by the program using these preferences can be modified using the Detailing menu > Show / Edit Slab/Mat/Footing Detailing command . Rebar Detail Options Use the options on this area to choose whether all bars will be detailed, or whether only bars above the typical bar layout should be detailed. Typical Bars: These options are available when the Detail Bars Above Typical Bars option has been selected. You may specify the size and number for the typical bars in the top and bottom of the beam. Only Where Required vs. Along Full Length: These options determine if the typical reinforcement is provided along the full length of the beam on only in the locations where reinforcement is required. Enforce User Minimum Reinforcement Use these options to enter a user specified minimum reinforcement for the top and bottom of the slab / mat / footing. Integrity Rebars on Columns for Flat Slabs (only available on the Slabs tab) Use the settings in this area to control how an elevated slab handles reinforcement over columns. User Minimum Reinforcement for Waffles and Ribs (only available on the Slabs tab) Use the settings in this area to control how an elevated slab handles reinforcement in waffles or ribs. Add Rebar Around Openings (not available on the Footing tab) Use the settings in this area to control how a foundation slab handles reinforcement around openings in the mat. Edit Rebar Selection Rules This button will open the Rebar Selection Rules form which allows you to specify what size and spacing of bars to use. The options available in the form will depend on whether you clicked this button from the Slab, Mat or Footing tab. Combine Adjacent Short Span Bottom Bars (only available on the Slabs tab) Use these options to dictate the maximum length to use when you want to combine bars across adjacent short spans. Add Bottom Bars in Drop Panels (only available on the Slabs tab) Use these options to force bottom bars into drop panel areas and specify what bar sizes and spacing to use.

#### Rebar Selection Rules - Column Stacks  [Menus/Detailing/Rebar_Selection_Rules_-_Column_Stacks.htm]
Rebar Selection Rules - Column Stacks Rebar Selection Rules - Column Stacks C lick the Detailing Menu > Bar Selection and Curtailment Rules and select the Column Stack option to access the RC Column: Bar Layout and Selection Rules form. From that form, select the Rebar Selection Rules button. For columns, detailing type can be Non-seismic or Seismic . For example, Seismic is used for Columns with Framing Type specified as Special Sway (For ACI 318) or Ductile (IS 456-2000) in the ETABS model whereas Non-seismic is for other Framing Types. Note: Detailing can be carried out for a model with both seismic and non-seismic detailing type columns. Note: In Seismic detailing, an additional tie zones B and C are available. Bar Sizes: The Smallest Bar Size, Largest Bar Sizes , and the Preferred Bar Size can be specified for the longitudinal bars and for tie zones by selecting the bar size from the drop-down list. Note: To add more bar sizes to the drop-down lists, go to Define menu > Section Properties Reinforcing bar Sizes Bar Numbers and Spacing: Minimum and Maximum Number of Bars for each Longitudinal Bar Type can be specified by directly entering the values into the text boxes. Also the spacing factors for each tie zone can be specified. Notes: When area of the specified Preferred Bar Size is insufficient during detailing and in such cases if selection of a higher bar size is desired rather than increasing Bar Number , the user must specify Maximum Number of Bars for the required Bar Type. Note: Smaller rebar size can be enforced in the middle (Zone C) by specifying the Smallest Bar Size preferred for Zone C. Confinement Button for Seismic Detailing: Click the Confinement button to access the Confinement Seismic Detailing form. Confinement Zone Length can be specified as the minimum of factors based on column height, section size or overall length. The type of tie used for the Outer Hoop can be specified (90 or 135 degree). I nternal Tie information is also be specified. This includes options on whether or not to require internal ties, and information about those ties. Internal Tie Type (L, rectangle - 90 degrees, or rectangle - 135 degrees) Frequency of internal ties (Every Bar, Alternate Bars, or Every Third Bar). Note: Currently 100% of bars are spliced at specified locations. If column section in ETABS modal has specified as to be checked then program will retain the specified rebar arrangement. However, if section is specified to be designed then program will use the specified layers as a guide and select appropriate bars Confinement Button for Non-Seismic Detailing: The type of tie used for the Outer Hoop can be specified (90 or 135 degree). Internal Tie information is also be specified. This includes options on whether or not to require internal ties, and information about those ties. Internal Tie Type (L, rectangle - 90 degrees, or rectangle - 135 degrees) Frequency of internal ties (Every Bar, Alternate Bars, or Every Third Bar). Note: Currently 100% of bars are spliced at specified locations. If column section in ETABS modal has specified as to be checked then program will retain the specified rebar arrangement. However, if section is specified to be designed then program will use the specified layers as a guide and select appropriate bars..

#### Show Detailing  [Menus/Detailing/Show_Detailing.htm]
Show Detailing Show / Edit Detailing Form: Beam Detailing Editor, Slab/Mat/Footing Detailing Editor There are two ways to open the Detailing Editor window. Method 1: Click the Detailing menu > Concrete, Steel} Detailing > Run/Update {} command to bring up the detailing editor. Note: You may see a form that requires you to select the floors for which detailing should be performed. Method 2: This command is available only if the Start Detailing/Check command (i.e. Method 1) has previously been executed or if the model has saved detailing information from a previous session. Click the Detailing menu > Show / Edit {Beam, Slab/Mat/Footing, Column Stack, Wall Stack} Detailing command. This will bring up the Select Detailing Options form which allows you to choose between the following options: Clear the previous detailing and re-run the detailing using the current rules and model Retain the previous detailing and ignore any changes that have been made to the model or the detailing rules Retain the previous Detailing for any components that were manually edited. But, rerun the detailing with the current rules and model for other components. After you have selected OK to the Select Detailing Options, this will bring up the Detailing Editor form for Beams, Columns, Slabs/Mats/footings or Wall. These forms display in the active window detailing drawings or views. The Edit, View and Preferences menus allow you access to various controls over the detailing and views. Navigating the Detailing Editor Windows The image below shows the various areas of the Detailing editor windows with descriptions below describing the main features of each area. Main Window This window may be moved, resized, maximized, minimized, or closed using standard Windows operations. Refer to Windows help available on the Start menu for additional information about these items. Main Title Bar The main title bar includes the program and model names. The main title bar is highlighted when the program is in use. Move the main window by left clicking in the main title bar and holding down the mouse button as you drag the window around the computer screen. Menu Bar The menu bar contains the program's menus from which various commands can be selected to perform specific actions. Such as Edit, View, and Preferences. Edit Edit {Beam, Design Leg} Rebar: If you use the Detailing Explorer to select a specific Beam (or Wall, or design strip in a slab), you can use the Edit > Edit {Beam, Design Leg} Rebar to bring up the Rebar Editing table for Walls, Beams or Slabs at the bottom of the Detailing Editor . Note: The Edit menu is not available in column stack version of the Detailing Editor. Instead, you may use the Detailing Explorer to select the specific column you wish to edit, then use the Right Click menu and select the Edit Column option to bring up the Rebar Editing table for the column Relabel Beams / Relabel Beam Groups: Only available in the beam version of the Detailing Editor , these menu options allow you to relabel a specific beam or beam group. This is done by first selecting the Beam Groups or the Story from the Detailing Explorer . Edit Beam Groups: Similar to the Edit Rebar commands, this command will bring up a Beam Group Editing table at the bottom of the Detailing Editor . This table is similar to the Rebar Editing window described in the first bullet point above. Update Beam Groups: This feature can be used to regroup beams after editing rebars of beams. View The View Menu give you standard controls to control the detail and section views including various Zoom controls, Pan , 3D Rotate and such. Also included are the ability to increase the display size of any text that appear in the view. Preferences Bar Selection and Curtailment Rules: This menu selection opens the Bar Selection and Curtailment Rule form for Beam , Column Stack , Wall Stack and Slab/Mat/Footing . Refer to each topic for more information about the controls available on those forms. Display Preferences: This menu selection opens the Display Preferences form for Beam , Column Stack , Wall Stack and Slab/Mat /Footing . Refer to each topic for more information about the controls available on those forms. Toolbars and Buttons Toolbars are made up of buttons. Buttons provide "single-click" access to commonly used commands. Holding the mouse pointer over a toolbar button for a few seconds without clicking or holding down any mouse buttons will display a short description of the button's function in a small text box. Detailing Explorer The detailing explorer displays the rebar details with the functionality to edit and view the rebar detailing. It has two main components namely Beam Rebar Details and Beam Views (For Beam) and Slab/Mats/Footing Rebar Details and Slab/Mat/Footing Views (for Slab/Mat/Footing). Items under Beam Rebar Details are useful for editing of rebars, view rebar quantities, edit labels etc. whereas items under Beam Views are for viewing purpose only. Similar definition is true for Slab/Mat/Footing Rebar Details and Slab/Mat/Footing Views. Also, there is an option to view the detailing output in 3D. This explorer allows easy access to details of slabs, mats, footings, and beams, including standard detailing results in graphical formats. Detailing Explorer (Slab / Mat / Footing) Items under Slab/Mat/Footing Editor are useful for editing of rebars, view rebar quantities, edit labels etc. If the user expands this parent node, multiple child nodes can be opened such as Rebars in Strips and Similar Rebars. This section is very interactive as the user can see the changes being made instantly in the Detailing View. Rebars in Strips: When user clicks a Rebars in Strips node, it shows the strip label, detailing type, total rebar length, weight etc. This node enables the user to check/modify the provided rebars (Bar Size, Spacing, Length etc.) over supports and spans for respective layer of strips. Support rebars are either A, A and B or C, C and D whereas Span rebars are F, F and G. Similar Rebars: This node enables the user to check/modify the provided rebars (User Label, Bar Size, Spacing etc.) for the similar bar groups. Rebars with the same bar type (A, A and B, C etc.), same bar size and spacing are grouped together and can be viewed and edited under this node. Similar Rib Groups: This node appears for the slabs that have ribs/waffles. Rebars in ribs or waffles with the same bar size and numbers are grouped together and can be viewed under this node. Detailing Explorer (Beams) The Beam Detailing Editor are useful for editing of rebars, view rebar quantities, edit labels etc. If the user expands this parent node, multiple child nodes can be opened such as Supports, Spans, and Sections. This section is very interactive as the user can see the changes being made instantly in the Detailing View . Supports: This node enables the user to check/modify the provided rebars (Bar Size, Number, Length etc.) over supports. Support rebars are A, B, C, or D for nonductile beams and A, B, C, D, F, G, H and J for ductile beams. Spans: This node enables the user to check/modify the provided rebars (Bar Size, Number, Length etc.) for the longitudinal bars. Span rebars are E, F, or G for nonductile beams. Similarly, the user can also check/modify the provided rebars (Bar Size, Spacing, Length etc.) for the longitudinal bars. Span rebars are E, F, or G for nonductile beams. Similarly, the user can also check/modify the provided rebars (Bar Size, Spacing, Length etc.) for the transverse bars (stirrups) with various available zones from Zone A to Zone E. Sections: This node enables the user to view/modify the Section cut in the respective Model. The user can specify the location for the section cut going to Property Grid. Important Note: Required longitudinal bars and stirrups bars for beams include required torsion reinforcement as well. Provided shear rebar area is calculated using the exact spacing value shown in the Property Grid and not the rounded value shown in views. Items under Beam Views are viewing purpose only. If the user expands this parent node, multiple child nodes can be opened such as Elevation (with Bars/No Bars), Rebar Profiles, Tendon Profiles, Section, and 3D view. Section: This node enables the user to view the Section cuts in the respective Model. 3D view: This node enables the user to view the rebar layout of the Model in a 3D view. User can zoom-in/out, move around and view the layout of rebar in the Model. Along with that, user can also show/hide the concrete surface, longitudinal bars, stirrups, tendon if present as well as set the desired colors for longitudinal bars stirrups, and also for tendons and anchors if present. Beam Groups: This node enables the user to check/modify the provided rebar details (Group Label, Beam Label, Concrete Cover, etc.) for the similar bar groups. Under Rebar Details , story by story rebar details for columns can be accessed. This section is very interactive as the user can see the changes being made instantly in the Detailing View . Column Views are for viewing purpose only. If the user expands this node, multiple child nodes can be opened such as Elevation (Full Elevation on 2 and 3 local directions), Section, and Full 3D view. Vertical Bars: This node enables the user to check/modify the provided vertical rebars (Bar Size, Spacing, Tie Shapes etc.) along the story height using the property grid. Tie Zones: This node enables the user to check/modify the provided tie rebars (Bar Sizes, Number of bars along 2 and 3 directions, Bar Selection Mode etc.) along the story height using the property grid.. Story>Spandrels>Spandrel number: This node enables the user to check/modify the provided spandrel rebars (Longitudinal Top, Middle and Bottom Bar Sizes and Numbers, Transverse Stirrup Size and Spacing etc.) along the story height, using the property grid.. #### Slab Display Preferences  [Menus/Detailing/Slab_Display_Preferences.htm]
Slab Display Preferences Slab Display Preferences The Display Preferences for the Detailing Editor provides the ability to control the display of the various plan, elevation, and section views available from the Detailing Editor. Plan View Options The controls on this tab apply to any plan view displays, including strip views. Visible in Plan The controls in the Visible in Plan group box applies to all plan views. The Visible in Section group box, while on the Plan View Options tab only applies to section detail views. Grids and Lines: The options in this area give you the ability to control the display of grid lines, section lines, beam edges and such. Objects: The options in this area give you control over the display of slab openings, columns, beams and walls. Labels: The options in this area allow you to turn the display of slab labels on or off. Properties: You can turn on or off the display of slab properties like concrete strength or thickness. Steel / Composite Beam Properties : You can turn on or off the display of certain beam properties within the plan view of your slab using the controls in this section. Visible in Section The controls in the Visible in Section group box applies to all section detail views of the slab. Grids and Lines: Turn on or off the display of the Grid Lines in the section view. Objects: You can turn on or off the display of certain reinforcing bars. Properties: You can turn on or off the display of slab thickness. Strip View Options These options control the display of the various types of strip views. There are multiple types of strip views: Plan Layout, Bar views (top, bottom, top and bottom), and Rebar profile. Grids and Lines: The support line option applies to all types of strip views. The show unit in dimension lines only applies to the plan layout type of strip view. Objects: The options in this area give you control over the display of columns, beams and walls in the strip views. Bars: The options in this area control the display of bars in the layout or profile views respectively. Properties: These options control the display of various lengths and dimensions in the strip views. Rebar Calls Rebar Calls in Plan: These options control the way the reinforcement is called out or displayed in the plan views, but does not affect the strip or section views. Rebar Calls in Section: These options control the way the reinforcement is called out or displayed in the section views of the slab, but does not affect the strip or plan views.

#### Slab Rebar Curtailment Rules  [Menus/Detailing/Slab_Rebar_Curtailment_Rules_Form.htm]
Slab Rebar Curtailment Rules Slab Rebar Curtailment Rules Form Use th e Slab Rebar Curtailment Rules form to specify the rules to be applied in detailing slab reinforcement. Use the form to specify parameters for the top and bottom bars at different locations.The data that can be modified includes: The Shape of the end hooks to be used.Select Straight, 90 deg bend or 180 hook. The length of the curtailed bar as a proportion of the clear or center-to-center span length. The percentage of total reinforcement to be curtailed at the specified length. Separate rules can be defined for slabs middle strips and columns strips, with or without drop panels, using the combo box at the top. This scheme is similar to the rules specified in various design codes. Note: The changes in the curtailment rules may not affect the final detailing of bars directly due to the consideration of computed bar cut-off locations, development and minimum bar length limits, etc. Bar Selection and Curtailment Rules can also be changed in the Detailing Window The detailing window can also be referred to as the "Slab/Mat/Footing Detailing Editor". Access the Slab Rebar Curtailment Rules form as follows: Click the Detailing menu > Bar Selection and Curtailment Rule > Slab/Mat/Footing Bar Selection and Curtailment Rule command to display the Slabs/Mats Detailing Preferences form. On the General and Display tab, choose the Apply Curtailment Rules option and click the Modify/Show Rules button.

Based on Rules - This option means the boundary zones will be detailed according to the rules set below: Use Boundary Zones vs Use Confinement Zones: This choice dictates wether your boundary zone will have closed ties to create confinement which may be required for seismic design. Default Boundary Length Ratio: Specified as a ratio of the boundary zone length to the pier length . Minimum Boundary Length: The boundary zone length is not allowed to be smaller than this minimum length. Specified using length units.

#### Acceleration-Displacement Response Spectrum (ADRS)  [Menus/Display/Acceleration_Displacement_Response_Spectrum_ADRS_.htm]
Acceleration-Displacement Response Spectrum (ADRS) Acceleration-Displacement Response Spectrum (ADRS) In the ADRS (Acceleration-Displacement Response Spectrum) format both the structural capacity (pushover) curve and the demand spectra are plotted in spectral-acceleration versus spectral-displacement coordinates. Refer to ATC-40 page 8-12 for additional information, including reference to the origin of this term.

#### Beam Information Form - Assignments Tab  [Menus/Display/Beam_Information_Form_-_Assignments_Tab.htm]

See the Frame Nonlinear Hinges form for more information. Pier - Identified if the frame object has a pier assignment . Spandrel - Identifies if the frame object has a spandrel assignment . Material Overwrites - Identifies if a material overwrite has been assigned to a selected frame object. Auto Mesh Type - Indicates if automatic frame subdivide assignments have been made to joints/frames/edges. Include in Analysis Mesh - Identifies if the frame object should be used (Yes or No) to mesh a floor shell object. See Frame Floor Meshing Option for more information. Groups - Identifies a group to which the line object has been assigned. Access the {Frame, Beam, Column, Brace} Information form by moving the cursor onto the object as if to select it, and then clicking the right mouse button rather than the left mouse button. #### Deformed Shape  [Menus/Display/Deformed_Shape.htm]
Deformed Shape Deformed Shape Form: Deformed Shape Deformed shapes display the loading on a model graphically. Note: Click the Apply button to update the active window. When the Apply button is clicked, the Deformed Shape form will remain open until it is closed by clicking the Close button. This allows selection of another frame object(s) for which a deformation may be displayed. If only one deformed shape is being displayed, the OK button can be used to both display the shape and close the form. TIP: Deformed shape can also be active by pressing the F6 keyboard shortcut. Run an analysis (see Set Load Cases to Run ). Click the Display menu > Deformed Shape command or the Show Deformed Shape button, , to access the Deformed Shape form. The Deformed Shape form has the following options: Load Case/ Load Combination / Modal Case: Use these radio buttons and drop down lists to choose the load case to be plotted. Note that a deformed shape can be plotted for Dead and Live load cases as well as any of the following, assuming that the type of load case or combination has been defined in the model. Static load case (linear) option. When a static load case is chosen, ETABS plots the deformed shape multiplied by a scale factor (see below). Response spectrum case option. When a response spectrum case is chosen, ETABS plots the deformed shape multiplied by a scale factor (see below). The deformed shape alone has little meaning because the response spectrum analysis causes all results (deformations) to be positive, and the displacements at each point are the maximum displacement at that point, which may not occur at the same time in an earthquake as the maximum displacement at another point. It can be useful to compare the deformed shape plot for a response spectrum with the undeformed shape to identify which parts of the structure are experiencing the most displacement. Time history case option. When a time history case is chosen, input a value in the Time edit box to specify the time step in the time history analysis to be displayed by the deformed shape. A deformed shape multiplied by a scale factor is plotted for the chosen time of the time analysis. If the time value specified is before the time history starts, the first step of the time history is displayed. If the time value specified is after the time history finishes, the last step of the time history is displayed. If the time value specified does not match exactly with one of the output time step times, the nearest time step is displayed. Nonlinear static case option. When a nonlinear static case is chosen, input a value in the Step edit box to specify the step in the nonlinear static analysis to be displayed by the deformed shape. A deformed shape multiplied by a scale factor is plotted for the chosen step of the nonlinear static analysis. Use the following steps to get an idea of the force and deformation associated with any step in the pushover: Click the Display menu > Static Pushover Curve command to access the Pushover Curve - Case {Name} form. Click the File menu at the top of that form. Click the Display Tables command to display a table that, among other things, includes the force and deformation for each step of the nonlinear static analysis. Load Combination Option: When a load combination is chosen, ETABS plots the deformed shape multiplied by the scale factor (see below). The relative meaning of the deformed shape depends on what is in the load combination. If the load combination is a single-valued load combination, the displayed results are meaningful. If the load combination is multi-valued, the displayed results have little meaning. In that case the value with the largest absolute value is displayed. For example if the minimum value at point 1 is -3 and the maximum value is +2, the -3 value is displayed. If an adjacent point has a minimum value of -1 and a maximum value of +2, then +2 is displayed at that point. This process continues for every point and can lead to some funny looking deformed shape plots. Modal Case Option: When a modal case is chosen, input a value in the Mode Number edit box to specify the mode to be displayed by the deformed shape. A deformed shape multiplied by a scale factor is plotted for the chosen mode number of the modal analysis. Scaling: Specify the scaling that is to be used to plot the deformed shape. By default ETABS automatically determines the scaling factor for the plot. Automatic option. ETABS automatically determines a scaling factor for the deformed shape plot by calculating the scale factor as a multiple of the default font size, which itself is determined as a multiple of the average story height. The advantage to determining the scale factor as a multiple of the default font size is that the default font size is limited by a specified minimum and maximum size that is specified in the graphic preferences . This helps keep the automatically determined scale factor within a reasonable range most, but not all, of the time. If the automatic scale factor seems to cause a display problem, use the other option and specify a Scale Factor. User Defined option and Scale Factor edit box. When this option is selected, use the edit box to specify a scale factor. If a scaling factor of 100 is specified, all deformations are plotted to scale at 100 times their actual value. For example, a deformation of 1 inch is plotted to scale as if it is a 100-inch deformation. Contour Contours: Draw Displacement Contours on Objects check box. Check this check box to draw contours of the displacement of the structure on the affected objects of the structure. Contour Component options. Choose which contour component to display on the model. Only one component at a time can be displayed. Contour Range values. Choose the minimum and maximum value range for displaying the contour. Options: Wire Shadow check box. When this check box is checked, the "wire shadow" is a line diagram of the undeformed shape. Cubic Curve check box. Specify if the cubic curve function should be used when plotting the deformed shape. Cubic curves affect how the line objects with frame section properties appear in the deformed shape plot. The cubic curve feature affects only line objects with frame section properties. ETABS saves only point/joint displacements from an analysis. Thus, when it prepares to plot a deformed shape, the only deformations it has available are the point/joint deformations. No deformations internal to the frame objects are available. When the deformed shape is plotted, the points/joints are put in their correct locations. If cubic curves are specified to not be considered, the frame elements are simply drawn as straight lines connecting the appropriate points/joints. If cubic curves are specified to be considered, ETABS does the following: Calculates an approximate deflection (translation and rotation at the center of the beam). Draws a cubic curve from the left end of the beam to the center of the beam based on the actual translation and rotation at the left end and the approximate translation and rotation at the center. Draws a cubic curve from the center of the beam to the right end of the beam based on the approximate translation and rotation at the center and the actual translation and rotation at the left end. Drawing a single cubic curve from the left end to the right end of the beam does NOT give a very good representation of a loaded beam, but using two curves, as is the case in ETABS , gives a pretty good plot. Nevertheless, when plotting a deformed shape, keep in mind that the displacements at the joints are exact, whereas deformation shown for the frame members is approximate, even when the cubic curve option is activated. Note: When a deformed shape is displayed, use the arrow keys on the status bar, , to step through the deformed shapes for the linear or nonlinear static load cases, the response spectrum cases, and the load combinations or the time steps in a time history analysis for a time history case. Display Joint Displacement: With a deformed shape displayed, right click on any point/joint object to access the Point Displacements form . Animation: When a deformed shape is displayed, click on the Start Animation button on the status bar to animate the deformed shape. Sometimes this makes it easier to recognize the deformed shape. Click the Stop Animation button on the status bar to stop the animation. Note that ETABS includes sound with the animation. Use the Options menu > Animation Sound command to toggle this sound on and off. See Also Output Colors

#### Energy Virtual Work Diagram  [Menus/Display/Energy_Virtual_Work_Diagram.htm]
Energy Virtual Work Diagram Energy / Virtual Work Diagram Form: Energy/Virtual Work Diagram Click the Display menu > Energy/Virtual Work Diagram command to display energy diagrams that can be used as an aid to determine which elements should be stiffened to achieve the most efficient control over the lateral displacements of a structure. Forces and Displacement drop-down list. Use the drop-down lists to select the load case associated with the forces and displacements to be displayed. Show Values check box. Check this check box and values (text) will be added to the graphical display. Click the Apply button to update the active window. When the Apply button is used, the Energy/Virtual Work Diagram form will remain open until the Close button is clicked. This allows another selection to be made on the form to review multiple displays without using the command to recall the form. If only one work diagram is to be displayed, the OK button can be used to both update the active window and close the form. Consider the two story structure shown in Figure "a" that has lateral loads P 1 and P 2 at the Roof and Second story levels, respectively. Also note the displaced shape, D , associated with this structure and loading, which is shown as a dashed line. Now consider the same structure, shown in Figure "b", with a single load P (typically a unit load) applied to it and a resulting displaced shape, d , shown as a dashed line. Maxwell's Reciprocal Theorem states that: P D = P 1 d roof + P 2 d second See a structural analysis textbook for details on Maxwell's Reciprocal Theorem. In this very simple example, the equation above could be reduced to an element level where the elements are illustrated in Figure "c" as: P D = [ P 1 d roof - P 1 d second ] + [( P 1 + P 2 ) d second - ( P 1 + P 2 ) d base ] Noting that d base is equal to zero, this equation reduces to: P D = [ P 1 d roof - P 1 d second ] + [( P 1 + P 2 ) d second ] In the preceding equation, the first term in brackets is the energy in the top element and the second term is the energy in the bottom element. The energy in both of these elements sums to the total P D energy. When the Display menu > Energy/Virtual Work Diagram command is used to display energy diagrams, ETABS reports the equivalent of the values shown in brackets in the last equation for each element in the structure. Note the following about the energy values that ETABS reports: They are based on all six degrees of freedom of the element, not just the one degree of freedom described in the Figure and the associated equations in the background information. They are determined as follows: ETABS determines the energy per unit volume associated with each element in the structure. ETABS normalizes all of the calculated energy values such that the largest one has a value of 100. As previously stated, the energy diagrams are helpful as an aid to determine which elements should be stiffened to control lateral displacements in a structure. In the preceding example, the required load case is shown in Figure "a." The load case associated with displacements is shown in Figure "b." Typically, this load case consists of one or more unit loads. The following figures show load cases that might be used for displacement load cases. Figure "d" shows a load case that is appropriate for controlling the roof displacement. Figure e shows a load case that is appropriate for controlling the interstory displacement between the roof and the second story level.

#### Hinge Results  [Menus/Display/Hinge_Results.htm]
Hinge Results Hinge Results Form: Hinge Response Use the Display menu > Hinge Results command to review a plot of plastic rotation vs moment, plastic deformation vs shear force, plastic deformation vs. axial force for a selected hinge. To display the Hinge Response form, first assign a hinge(s) to a frame object and define a nonlinear static load case whose Results Saved type is Multiple States. #### Joint Drifts  [Menus/Display/Joint_Drifts.htm]
Joint Drifts Joint Drifts Output Table One of the data table types that the program can accommodate is Story Drift. The program uses the general criteria for the calculation of the story drifts. Therefore, this value is the difference in lateral deformations between two stories, generated by lateral forces, divided by the difference in height between the two stories in question. The Story Drift table can be accessed as follows: From the Choose Tables form click the Analysis Results section > Joint Output > Displacements > Table: Story Drifts . Important Note: The program does not display all story drifts values in the output table. It only reports it when the value is above or equal to 20% of the one in the principal direction.

#### Load Assigns  [Menus/Display/Load_Assigns.htm]
Load Assigns Load Assigns Forms: Show Joint Loads, Show Frame Loads, Show Shell Loads, Show Tendon Loads Click the Display menu > Load Assigns > Joint, Display menu > Load Assigns > Frame, Display menu > Load Assigns > Shell, and the Display menu > Load Assigns > Tendon commands to display loads defined using the Define menu > Load Patterns command and assigned using the submenu commands of the Assign menu > Joint Loads , Assign menu > Frame Loads, Assign menu > Shell Loads, and the Assign menu > Tendon Loads commands. Display menu > Load Assigns > Joint command. Click this command to access the Show Joint Loads form, which has the following options: Load Pattern drop-down list. Choose the load patternwhose joint loads are to be displayed. Load Type options. Choose the type of load to be displayed. Only one load type can be displayed at a time. Show Loading Values check box. When this check box is unchecked, forces and displacements are indicated by arrows in the appropriate direction only. When this check box is checked, forces and displacements are indicated by arrows in the appropriate direction together with loading values (text). Loading values are always shown when the Temperature Values option has been selected in the Load Type area whether the Show Loading Values check box is checked or unchecked. Display menu > Load Assigns > Frame command to access the Show Frame Loads form, which has the following options: Load Pattern drop-down list. Choose the load pattern whose frame loads are to be displayed. Load Type options. Choose the type of load to be displayed. Only one load type can be displayed at a time. Also, if a load type is unavailable (grayed out), that type of load has not been assigned for the load pattern selected. Span Loading Applied Directly to the Frame Object (Forces) option. Includes all of the point, uniform and trapezoidal force loads (not moment loads) applied to the frame object. Span Loading Applied Directly to the Frame Object (Moments) option. Includes all of the point, uniform and trapezoidal moment loads applied to the frame object. All Loading that is Tributary to the Frame Object (Forces) option. Displays the calculated point, uniform and trapezoidal loads tributary to the frame object. All Loading that is Tributary to the Frame Object (Moments) option. Displays the calculated point, uniform and trapezoidal moment loads tributary to the frame object. Temperature Values option. Includes all of the temperature loads applied to the frame object. Important Note: When temperature loads are displayed, two numbers are shown for each frame object. Those two numbers correspond to the temperatures at the ends of the object. If the effects of joint temperature were specified to not be included when the temperature load was assigned (see Temperature Load - Frame Objects , Include Effects of Joint Temperatures check box unchecked), the two displayed temperatures for the frame object are the same and are equal to the temperature assigned to the object. This is true regardless of any joint object temperatures that may be assigned to the joint objects at the end of the frame object. If the effects of point temperature were specified to be included when the temperature load was assigned ( Include Effects of Joint Temperatures check box checked), the two displayed temperatures for the frame object are equal to the temperature assigned to the object plus the temperature assigned to the joint object at the considered end of the frame object (see Temperature - Joints ). In that case, the two displayed temperatures for a frame object may be different. Open Structure Wind Loads option. Includes the open structure wind loads applied to the frame object. Include Joint Object Loads check box. This check box toggles the display of joint object loads on or off. When this box is checked, both force and moment joint object loads are displayed along with the selected type of frame object loads. Show Loading Values check box. When this check box is unchecked, forces and moments are indicated by arrows in the appropriate direction only. When this check box is checked, forces and moments are indicated by arrows in the appropriate direction together with loading values (text). Loading values are always shown when the Temperature Values option is selected in the Load Type area whether the Show Loading Values check box is checked or unchecked. Display menu > Load Assigns > Shell command to access the Show Shell Loads form, which has the following options: Load Pattern drop-down list. Choose the load case whose shell loads are to be displayed. Load Type options. Choose the type of load to be displayed. Only one load type can be displayed at a time. Uniform Load Values option. The uniform surface load on a shell object. If this option is chosen, also specify the loading direction (e.g., gravity, Local 1, Local 2 and so on) for the loads by choosing a direction from the Direction drop-down list. Temperature Values option. Includes all of the temperature loads applied to the shell object. Important Note: When temperature loads are displayed, numbers are shown at each corner of the shell object. Those numbers correspond to the temperatures at the corners of the object. If the effects of joint temperature were specified to not be included when the temperature load was assigned (see Temperature ), the displayed temperatures for the shell object are the same and are equal to the temperature assigned to the object. This is true regardless of any joint object temperatures that may be assigned to the joint objects at the corners of the shell object. If the effects of joint temperature were specified to be included when the temperature load was assigned, the displayed temperatures for the shell object are equal to the temperature assigned to the object plus the temperature assigned to the joint object at the considered corner of the shell object. In that case the displayed temperatures for a shell object may be different at each corner. Wind Pressure option. The wind pressure coefficient and total force on an area object, in the W (Windward) or L (Leeward) direction. Display menu > Load Assigns > Tendon command to access the Show Tendon Loads form, which has the following options: Load Pattern drop-down list. Choose the load case whose tendon loads are to be displayed if post-tensioning is present in the model. Load Type options. Choose the type of load to be displayed. Only one load type can be displayed at a time. Tendon Assigned Loads option. This option displays the load assigned to the tendon. Tendon Calculated Loads option. This option displays the loads as imparted onto the slab from the tendon. Analysis Model Loads option. This option displays the loads transformed onto the elements of the analysis model. Show Loading Values check box. When this check box is checked, numeric load values are added to the display.

#### Point Displacements  [Menus/Display/Point_Displacements.htm]
Point Displacements Point Displacements The Point Displacements form displays the displacements (translation and rotation) and drifts (where appropriate) for that point object in the global coordinate system. The drifts are calculated as the displacement at that point minus the displacement at the point one story below the considered point (if one exists). Important Note: When an analysis is run, ETABS automatically creates a joint object at the center of mass of all rigid diaphragms. This joint object is restrained against translation in the Z-direction and against rotation about the global X and Y axes to be compatible with the rigid diaphragm. Right click on that point to see displacements at the center of mass of the diaphragm. Note that the Z translation and X and Y rotations for these center of mass points are zero because the joints are restrained. Also note, toggle the display of these center of mass joints on or off by checking or unchecking the Invisible/Joint Objects item in the Object Present in View area of the Set View Options form, which can be accessed using the View menu > Set Display Options command . Access the Point Displacements form as follows: Click the Display menu > Deformed Shape command or the Show Deformed Shape button, , to access the Deformed Shape form. With a deformed shape displayed, right click on any point/joint object .

#### Response Spectrum Curves  [Menus/Display/Response_Spectrum_Curves.htm]
Response Spectrum Curves Response Spectrum Curves Form: Response Spectrum Use the Display menu > Response Spectrum Curves command to display the response spectrum for a specified time history case. Important Note: The response spectrum plotted using this command is based on a previously run time history analysis. It has nothing to do with any response spectrum analysis that may have been run. To display a response spectrum curve, first define a time history function and a time history case and run an analysis. Then click the Display menu > Response Spectrum Curves command, which will display the Response Spectrum form. The form will display with a tab at the top, a tool bar, graphical plot and plot parameter options. Tab - The name of the Response Spectrum form displays. The Tool Bar Graphical Plot area. The plot is shown in this area with appropriate labeling for the X and Y axes. When the mouse pointer is moved over the plot, the coordinates of the pointer location are shown below the plot. Plot Parameters (i.e., Name, Show, Vertical Axis, Horizontal Axis, Frequencies/Periods) - Use the plot parameter options to set the plot display. Click on a parameter and an explanation of that parameter will display in the lower left-hand corner of the form. If the text of the parameter name is partially hidden, use the cursor to drag the parameter area to make it larger, similar to resizing in Windows or Mircosoft Excel. Similarly, if the text display area in the lower left-hand corner is too small, drag it up to make it larger. Changes to the parameters can be made by clicking the value area. The changes made to the parameters immediately update the graphical plot. Clicking the Damping Ratios item will display the button; clicking that button will display the Specified Damping Ratios form. Use the Specified Damping Ratios form to modify the damping values. Add a new item - Click this button to add an additional row and define another damping value to be displayed on the response spectrum plot. Add a copy of the selected item - Select a value in the list and click this button to add a copy of it to the form. Delete the selected item - Select a value in the list and click this button to delete it. Sort by the first column - Click this button to rearrange the listing of damping ratios based on the first column in the damping ratio table. Legend - Use the Legend drop-down list to specify no legend (None), a stand alone legend, or an integrated legend. The stand along legend displays beside the graphical plot area. The integrated legend lies within the graphical plot area.

#### Reactions Form  [Menus/Display/Show_Member_Force_and_Stress_Diagrams/Reactions_Form.htm]
Reactions Form Reactions Form The Reactions form has the following areas: Load Case/ Load Combination / Modal Case: Use these radio buttons and drop down lists to choose the load case, load combination, or modal case for which the support or spring reactions are to be displayed. Load Case Option: The support or spring reactions for any of the following can be plotted assuming that the type of load case has been defined in the model. Static load case (linear) option. When the Tabulated option is selected, the force values are displayed. When the arrows options is selected, the arrows indicate the direction of the force acting from the support (spring) on to the elements connected to the support (spring). Response spectrum case option. The reaction values are displayed along with arrows showing the direction of the force. The arrows indicate the direction of the force acting from the support (spring) on to the elements connected to the support (spring). Note that the response spectrum reaction show the maximum value obtained for each component of each reaction and also note that the values may not occur at the same time in an earthquake. Time history case option. When a time history case is chosen, use the edit box to specify the time step in the time history analysis to be plotted. If a time that is specified is before the time history starts, the first step of the time history is displayed. If a time is specified that is after the time history finishes, the last step of the time history is displayed. If a time is specified that is not exactly the same as one of the output time step times, the nearest time step is displayed. The reaction values are displayed along with arrows showing the direction of the force. The arrows indicate the direction of the force acting from the support (spring) on to the elements connected to the support (spring). Static nonlinear case option. When a static nonlinear case is chosen, use the edit box to specify the step in the static nonlinear analysis to be plotted. The reaction values are displayed along with arrows showing the direction of the force. The arrows indicate the direction of the force acting from the support (spring) onto the elements connected to the support (spring). Use the following steps to get an idea of the force and deformation associated with any step in the pushover: Click the Display menu > Static Pushover Curve command to access the Pushover Curve - Case {Name} form. Click the File menu at the top of the form. Click the Display Tables command to display a table that, among other things, includes the force and deformation for each step of the nonlinear static analysis. Load combination Option: Choose to display reactions for the load absolute maximum, maximum or minimum. Depending on the Plot Type option selected, the reactions can be displayed using arrows showing the direction of the force. The arrows indicate the direction of the force acting from the support (spring) onto the elements connected to the support (spring). If a load combination is a single-valued load combination, its reaction values are displayed. If a load combination is multi-valued, the displayed results are those with the largest absolute value. For example, if the minimum value at point 1 is -3 and the maximum value is +2, the -3 value is displayed. If an adjacent point has a minimum value of -1 and a maximum value of +2, then +2 is displayed at that point. This process continues for every component at every reaction point. Modal Case Option: When the Modal Case option is selected, choose the mode number for which reactions are to be displayed. Plot Type: Choose to display the reactions using Arrows or as Tabulated values. Display Result for These Components: Choose which reactions are to be displayed. The components are assumed to be self-explanatory. If more information is required, please consult the code-specific design manuals ( Help menu > Documentation command). Click the Apply button to update the active window. When the Apply button is used, the Reactions form will remain open until the Close button is clicked. This allows another selection to be made on the form to review multiple displays without using the command to recall the form. If only one Plot Type or Component is to be displayed, the OK button can be used to both update the active window and close the form. Access the Reactions form as follows: Run an analysis. Click the Display menu > Forces/Stresses Diagram > Support/Spring Reactions command. TIP: The Reactions form may also be activated by pressing the F7 keyboard shortcut.

#### Shell Forces Stresses Form  [Menus/Display/Show_Member_Force_and_Stress_Diagrams/Shell_Forces_Stresses_Form.htm]
Shell Forces Stresses Form Shell Forces/Stresses Form Important Note: The internal shell element forces are forces per unit length acting along the mid-surface of the shell element (area object). The internal shell element stresses are stresses acting on the edges (not positive 3-axis face and negative 3-axis face) of the shell element (area object). Note: Click the Apply button to update the active window using the parameters specified on the form. When the Apply button is used, the Shell Forces/Stresses form will remain open until the Close button is clicked. This allows another selection to be made on the form to review multiple displays without using the command to recall the form. The OK button can be used to both update the active window and close the form if only one view is needed. The Shell Forces/Stresses form has the following options: L oad Case/ Load Combination / Modal Case: Use these radio buttons and drop down lists to choose the load case, load combination, or modal case for which the shell element forces or stresses are to be displayed. Note that shell element forces or stresses can be plotted for any static load case, response spectrum case, time history case, static nonlinear case, or load combination. For time history cases, also specify a time for display of the forces or stresses. For static nonlinear cases, also specify a step for display of the forces or stresses. Component Type: Choose to display shell element internal forces , internal stresses , or strains. When stresses or strains are selected, also select the face of the shell object - visible, top, or bottom - for which values are to be displayed, or choose that the maximum, minimum or absolute maximum stress/strain values are to be displayed. Component Options: Specify the component of force or stress to be displayed. For shell element internal forces , the possible components are as follows: F11: Direct force per unit length acting at the mid-surface of the element on the positive and negative 1 faces in the 1-axis direction. F22: Direct force per unit length acting at the mid-surface of the element on the positive and negative 2 faces in the 2-axis direction. F12: Shearing force per unit length acting at the mid-surface of the element on the positive and negative 1 faces in the 2-axis direction, and acting on the positive and negative 2 faces in the 1-axis direction. FMax: Maximum principal force per unit length acting at the mid-surface of the element. Note that by definition principal forces are oriented such that the associated shearing force per unit length is zero. FMin: Minimum principal force per unit length acting at the mid-surface of the element. Note that by definition principal forces are oriented such that the associated shearing force per unit length is zero. FVM : Von Mises principal force per unit length acting at the mid-surface of the element. V13: Out-of-plane shear per unit length acting at the mid-surface of the element on the positive and negative 1 faces in the 3-axis direction. V23: Out-of-plane shear per unit length acting at the mid-surface of the element on the positive and negative 2 faces in the 3-axis direction. VMax: Maximum principal shear per unit length acting at the mid-surface of the element. Note that by definition principal shears are oriented on faces of the element such that the associated shears per unit length on perpendicular faces are zero. M11: Direct moment per unit length acting at the mid-surface of the element on the positive and negative 1 faces about the 2-axis . M22: Direct moment per unit length acting at the mid-surface of the element on the positive and negative 2 faces about the 1-axis . M12: Twisting moment per unit length acting at the mid-surface of the element on the positive and negative 1 faces about the 1-axis , and acting on the positive and negative 2 faces about the 2-axis. MMax: Maximum principal moment per unit length acting at the mid-surface of the element. Note that by definition principal moments are oriented such that the associated twisting moment per unit length is zero. MMin: Minimum principal moment per unit length acting at the mid-surface of the element. Note that by definition principal moments are oriented such that the associated twisting moment per unit length is zero. For shell element internal stresses, the possible components are as follows: S11: Direct stress (force per unit area) acting on the positive and negative 1 faces in the 1-axis direction. S22: Direct stress (force per unit area) acting on the positive and negative 2 faces in the 2-axis direction. S12: Shearing stress (force per unit area) acting on the positive and negative 1 faces in the 2-axis direction and acting on the positive and negative 2 faces in the 1-axis direction . SMax: Maximum principal stress (force per unit area). Note that by definition principal stresses are oriented such that the associated shearing stress is zero. SMin: Minimum principal stress (force per unit area). Note that by definition principal stresses are oriented such that the associated shearing stress is zero. SVM : Von Mises principal stress (force per unit area). S13: Out-of-plane shearing stress (force per unit area) acting on the positive and negative 1 faces in the 3-axis direction. S23: Out-of-plane shearing stress (force per unit area) acting on the positive and negative 2 faces in the 3-axis direction. SMaxV: Maximum principal shearing stress (force per unit area). Note that by definition principal shearing stresses are oriented on faces of the element such that the associated shears per unit length on perpendicular faces are zero. For shell element strains , the possible components are as follows: E11: Direct strain in the 1-axis direction. E22: Direct strain in the 2-axis direction. G12: Engineering shear strain in the 1-2 plane. EMAX: Maximum principal strain. Note that by definition, principal strains are oriented such that the associated shear strain is zero EMIN: Minimum principal strain. Note that by definition, principal strains are oriented such that the associated shear strain is zero EVM: Von Mises strain, also known as the equivalent strain. G13: Out-of-plane engineering shear strain in the 1-3 plane. G23: Out-of-plane engineering shear strain in the 2-3 plane. GMAXV: Maximum principal transverse shear strain. This is the vector resultant of G13 and G23 Contour Appearance: Use these options to choose if the forces and stresses will display on an Undeformed Shape , a Deformed Shape , or a display of an Extruded Contour by selecting an option from the drop-down list. Also use the Show Lines , Show Fill , Show Values , and Show Arrows check boxes to specify how the forces and stresses will be illustrated. The options are assumed to be self-explanatory. Contour Values: The shell element internal forces, stresses and strains are displayed on screen as colored contours. Specify minimum and maximum values: Min edit box: Any element with a force/stress/strain less than the value specified in this edit box is displayed in the color associated with Min in the Contours area of the Assign Display Colors form . Note that the color associated with Min is the top color in the form. Max edit box: Any element with a force/stress/strain greater than or equal to the value specified in this edit box is displayed in the color associated with Max in the Contours area of the Assign Display Colors form. Note that the color associated with Max is the bottom color in the form. With the Min and the Max values specified, ETABS spaces the intermediate range values equally between the specified Min and Max values. If the Min and the Max values are both set to zero, ETABS creates its own range. In that case, ETABS creates a stress range with rounded (even) values that the actual maximum and minimum stresses fit within. Note that setting Min and Max to zero is the default. Contour Averaging at Nodes. Specify if stress averaging is to be used when displaying the shell element forces or stresses. ETABS offers the following options: None - no stress averaging By Objects - stress averaging at all objects By Selected Groups - stress averaging at specific points selected just before plotting the shell forces or stresses; click the Groups button to access the Select Groups form and select objects by Group names. Explanation of Contour Averaging Consider the four shell elements labeled A, B, C and D shown in the sketch below. These four shell elements all have a common point, labeled 1, in the sketch. Each of the shell elements has an associated internal force, stress or strain at joint 1. Typically the values at common points in the various shell elements are different. The finer the mesh, the closer the values become. If the force/stress/strain contours are plotted with no stress averaging at the common points, typically the changes in value from element to element will be abrupt. Stress averaging tends to eliminate the abrupt changes in the plot and smooths the contours. ETABS averages the stresses at a point by averaging the stresses from all shell elements that both connect to the point and are visible in the active window . Then when ETABS plots the stress for a particular shell element, it plots that average stress at the point considered instead of the actual stress calculated for that shell element at the point. Do not overlook the implications of the underlined portion of the previous paragraph. For example, assume the active window is displaying stresses in a location where a wall intersects a floor. Further assume that the display shows averaged stresses in the floor. If the averaged stresses in the floor are displayed in a 2D plan view of the floor, only the shell elements that are in the floor, and thus visible in the window, are included in the stress averaging. If the same averaged stresses are displayed in a 3D view, where both the wall and the floor are visible, the shell elements from both the floor and the wall are included in the stress averaging. Thus the averaged stresses in the floor at the intersection of the floor and the wall will appear differently in a 2D plan view versus a 3D view. Scaling: The scaling options will be available only if Display on Deformed Shape or Display Extruded Contours has been selected for the Contour Option . When available, the scale factor can be used to exaggerate the displacements/extrusions relative to the geometry of the structure. Choose Automatic scaling or specify a User Scale Factor to scale the deformed shape or the extruded results. Miscellaneous Notes about Shell Element Forces, Stresses and Strains: Shell element stresses or strains (not forces) actually have different values at the top and bottom of the shell elements (area objects). Thus, depending on which side of the object is displayed, different stresses may be shown. Two-dimensional views always display area objects from the same side. To display stresses on the other side of the area object, view them in a 3D view. Finally, when shell element forces, stresses or strains are plotted for multi-valued load combinations, ETABS displays the maximum or minimum value that has the largest absolute value. Access the Shell Forces/Stresses form as follows: Run an analysis. Click the Display menu > Force/Stress Diagrams > Shell Stresses/Forces command. TIP: The Shell Forces / Stresses form may also be activated by pressing the F9 keyboard shortcut.
